# Sparse View and Few-Shot Optimization
## Overview
Sparse View and Few-Shot Optimization addresses the severe artifacts, overfitting, and geometry breakdown that occur when training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with a drastically reduced number of input viewpoints ($|S| < 20$) [S1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF training by introducing specialized regularization, data densification, or geometric constraints to mitigate the ambiguity inherent in limited observations, rather than relying on large-scale pre-training or external depth priors [S1, unofficial].
## Shared principles
All methods in this family optimize a radiance field $F_\Theta$ from a sparse set of input views ($|S| < 20$) without large-scale pre-training, employing auxiliary supervision, geometric constraints, or pseudo-data generation to mitigate overfitting and geometry breakdown [S1, unofficial].
## Subtopics

### [Simple-NeRF](7371-simple-nerf.md)
Simple-NeRF is a regularization method for sparse-input Neural Radiance Fields that employs two simpler augmented NeRF models (points and views augmentations) to provide depth supervision to the main NeRF, mitigating overfitting and implausible geometries caused by high capacity and sparse views. It sets itself apart from prior works by obtaining depth supervision through augmented models trained in-situ without requiring pre-training on large datasets or external depth models. Choose this method when the base model achieves reasonable performance but suffers from distortions or transparent floaters due to sparse inputs.

### [WaH-NeRF](11548-wah-nerf.md)
WaH-NeRF is a training framework for Neural Radiance Fields from sparse inputs that mitigates rendering confusion by addressing two root causes: sample-position confusion ("WHERE to Sample?") and prediction confusion ("HOW to Predict?"). It sets itself apart from sibling methods by analyzing the sample-render process and mitigating confusion before volume rendering, rather than relying on regularization for rendered color and depth images after volume rendering. Choose this method when rendering confusion from sparse inputs causes geometry breakdown and inconsistent surface predictions.

### [Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS](11859-deceptive-nerf-3dgs.md)
Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS is a sparse-view reconstruction method that densifies limited input observations by generating photorealistic pseudo-observations via a 2D diffusion model, treating them as real training views to overcome overfitting and artifacts inherent in few-view settings. It sets itself apart from sibling methods that use diffusion models as per-step regularizers by inferring the diffusion model only during a dedicated generation phase, drastically reducing computational cost while improving reconstruction quality. Choose this method when input views are extremely sparse and standard pipelines suffer from severe artifacts, and computational budget allows for a dedicated generation phase.

### [FlipNeRF](12967-flipnerf.md)
FlipNeRF is a regularization framework for few-shot novel view synthesis that generates auxiliary "flipped reflection rays" from original input rays and estimated surface normals to improve rendering quality and surface normal accuracy with sparse inputs. It sets itself apart from Ref-NeRF by generating additional training rays rather than reparameterizing the radiance field's input viewing direction, and distinguishes itself from pre-training methods by optimizing per-scene without large-scale priors. Choose this method when surface normal accuracy and geometric consistency are critical for few-shot synthesis.

### Few-shot NeRF
#### definition
- NeRF represents a scene as a continuous function $F_\theta(\cdot)$ implemented by a neural network with parameters $\theta$, taking 3D coordinates $\mathbf{x}$ and viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$ with positional encoding $\gamma(\cdot)$ to output color $\mathbf{c}$ and density $\sigma$ [S1, unofficial].
#### parameter
- Few-shot NeRF setting: number of input viewpoints $|S|$ is drastically reduced to a few viewpoints, specifically $|S| < 20$ [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The term "Few-shot NeRF" was introduced to describe scenarios where the number of input viewpoints is drastically reduced from the standard hundreds to fewer than 20, leading to high divergent behaviors such as geometry breakdown and artifacts [S1, unofficial]. The DaRF paper [S1, unofficial] explores this setting, noting that existing frameworks applied regularization techniques at unknown viewpoints to constrain NeRF with additional 3D priors, though with limited performance.

## Sources
[S1] DaRF: Boosting Radiance Fields from Sparse Inputs with Monocular Depth Adaptation, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.19201, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
